author: Morten Hertzum
comment: As I understand it, what we aim to check is whether the about 60 scenarios were correctly auto-analyzed in Track 1. So, we would want to state how many times each of the ~60 scenarios were checked by a human participant in Track 2. Discounting variation from the random selection of trials from the full set, I suppose it is #Participants * #Trials pr participant / #Scenarios. In the paper, we can report the actual range.

author: Morten Hertzum
comment: It is not clear to me what we are asking participants to assess (probaby because it is unclear to me whether Track 1 determined the ground truth for recommendations or explanations). I initially thought we were asking participants to assess the AI recommendation (in this case: “The strongest alternative is OAML”). However, the questions in Figure 3 instruct the participants to assess the explanation. In Figure 2, the recommendation matches the rank of OAML in the reference rank column and, thus, appears correct. In contrast, part of the explanation, does not match the runtime column (15.03s vs 8.53s for ChaCha) and, thus, appears incorrect. In addition, Figure 2 presents both the recommendation and the explanation under the heading “AI explanation” making it impossible for the participant to tell them apart. The first sentence (“The scenario prioritizes Accuracy and Runtime and Energy”) merely restates the task and therefore does not explain. The second sentence concludes that ChaCha “ranks #1” and provides an explanation for that conclusion. The third sentence recommends “OAML” and provides an explanation for that recommendation. I am worried that what was presented as ‘explanations’ in the ground-truth assessment in Track 1 differs from how participants in Track 2 come to understand ‘explanations’ on the basis of the interface in Figure 2 and 3. If so, the Track 1 assessments do not provide a good benchmark against which to compare the participants’ ratings in Track 2.Is it also not clear to me (and may therefore also be unclear to participants) what status the information in the “Scenario -> Task -> Evidence connection” list has. Is it information independent of AwareML, available to AwareML, or from AwareML? If it is independent of AwareML, then participants should understand that it is not part of the ”AI assistant” they are asked to assess. If it is available to AwareML, then there must be other information available as well (otherwise the runtime for ChaCha would not mismatch), thereby raising questions about whether the table contains authoritative information. If it is from AwareML, then it is hard to understand that a mismatch like the one for ChaCha runtime can occur.

author: Morten Hertzum
comment: The accept/override/reject decision is currently ambiguous because it is about ”this recommendation / explanation”. The participant may accept the recommendation but reject (part of) the explanation. We need to know whether they are accepting/overriding/rejecting one or the other. I suggest asking ”What would you do with this recommendation?” Like above, this requires that the interface distinguishes more clearly between recommendations and explanations.Whether or not participants seek optional evidence is a good indicator of whether the AI recommendation and explanation (in Figure 2) has convinced the participant

author: Morten Hertzum
comment: We should test how the answer to this question relates to whether the participant sought optional evidence (in Figure 4)

author: Morten Hertzum
comment: AwareML considers four priorities/objectives: accuracy, energy, CO2, and runtime. This scenario shows that there are more objectives (in this scenario security/privacy). How is the incompleteness of the four included objectives factored into the study? Is correctness/incorrectness in the ground truth-assessment relative to the four objectives only? If so, the ground truth is only applicable to the trials in Track 2 and 3 if participants in Track 2 and 3 are also disregarding objectives beyond the four included. Do/can we ensure that?If correctness/incorrectness in the ground truth-assessment is relative to all scenario-relevant objectives (i.e., possibly more/others than the four included objectives), what does it mean that the “scenario context” field states “scenario priorities: Accuray”? - it comes across as a factual statement about the scenario, not as, for example, a result produced by the AI.In what way is the “Initial AwareML recommendation” initial? -> can the participant provide input that leads AwareML to recompute and potentially make another recommendation? If not, I suggest removing ‘initial’.Is Utility (in the table) the weighted average of the four objectives, i.e., is it the paramenter that defines the ranking? If so, it appears identical to the “Scenario fit score” in Figure 2 and should have the same name. If not, why do the tables in Figure 2 and the present figure have different columns?The “What would you change?” field: Can the participants’ explorations give them any evidence that will enable them to suggest new values for accuracy, runtime… or are they, rather, being asked whether they would give more (or less) weight to some of the objectives in the calculation of the frameworks’ rank? The participant can indicate one option only, so it appears that we are asking “What would you most want to change?”
